children: Two of the retail sector's biggest comeback stories over the last year are Target Corporation
. While the retailers took different routes in recovering their business, the common factor was decisive actions by a new CEO.

has turned its momentum around this year after posting negative comparable sales in three straight fiscal years and seeing its share price plunge. The promotion of longtime insider Michael Fiddelke to the CEO position saw a shift in priorities by the Minneapolis-based company. Fiddelke's strategy is about focus. He declared that Target

is not an everything store, and the company is aggressively remaking the home, baby, and beauty businesses. He reorganized merchandising leadership and committed $2B to store renovations, merchandising overhauls, and technology upgrades. The plan also included big cost cuts, including the company's largest corporate layoffs in a decade. Under his tenure, Target
has leaned on digital growth and high-margin advertising as well.

recovery has been even more explosive after tariff fears, soft guidance, a security breach, and an activist campaign muddied the waters for investors. CEO Hillary Super's playbook was a return to basics. She reasserted the brand's authority in bras while growing Pink, beauty, and sport and reimagined marketing. Notably, the bras business posted low double-digit comparable growth. Super also pushed a full-price selling strategy rather than training shoppers to wait for markdowns. Under Super, Victoria's Secret (VSCO) has recorded five consecutive quarters of positive comparable sales. Super also won her fight with activist BBRC International, which voted against every board nominee except Super herself.
In a sector crowded with struggling brands and worries about cautious consumer spending, Target
have turned the corner and attracted investor interest in their turnaround stories.

title: Target and Victoria's Secret: Two of retail's biggest turnaround stories
